problem_statement: The paper frames the problem as modeling and analyzing continuous-time stochastic processes, especially when analytic solutions are unavailable and numerical methods become expensive. In the finance setting, it highlights option pricing with discontinuous price movements and other path-dependent or history-sensitive quantities such as ruin probability.
problem_statement_quotes:
Modeling stochastic phenomena in continuous time is an essential yet chal-
lenging problem.

Analytic solutions are often unavailable, and numerical meth-
ods can be prohibitively time-consuming and computationally expensive.

Illustrative examples in-
clude option pricing in the Merton Jump Diffusion Model and ruin probability
computing in the Collective Risk Model, showcasing the framework’s ability
to capture extreme market events and incorporate history-dependent informa-
tion.
classical_baseline: The paper compares against classical numerical methods, especially Monte Carlo simulation, and against the Black-Scholes model in option pricing. It also treats the original Black-Scholes formula as the standard baseline for European option pricing.
classical_baseline_quotes:
Moreover, the application of numerical methods like Monte Carlo
simulation can be computationally demanding, requiring unexpectedly large storage and
computation resources.

The famous Black-Scholes model is proposed to evaluate a European option [41], and the simulation
for Black-Scholes type option pricing has been implemented on quantum computers [29–
31, 33].

Instead of a Brownian motion in the Black-Scholes
model, one has to simulate, in the Merton Jump Diffusion Model, the more complicated
case of a Lévy process where our method can be applied to make a quadratic speed-up
against the classical Monte Carlo simulation.
classical_difficulty: The paper says the classical difficulty comes from the continuous path structure: analytic formulas are often unavailable, and Monte Carlo simulation needs unexpectedly large storage and computation because the sampling space grows exponentially as time slices get finer. For finance, it also notes that discontinuous returns and path dependence make the standard Black-Scholes setting less realistic and harder to handle.
classical_difficulty_quotes:
Analytic solutions or explicit formulas
for the underlying stochastic differential equations and quantities are often unavailable
for practical problems.

Moreover, the application of numerical methods like Monte Carlo
simulation can be computationally demanding, requiring unexpectedly large storage and
computation resources.

This is primarily due to the exponential growth of the sampling
space as time slices become finer, and the intricate nature of the evolution dynamics within
the process [6, 7].

However, the assumption of a constant variance log-normal distribution in the
original article [41] turns out to be less realistic as the empirical studies of discontinuous
returns of stock are ignored.
business_stakes: The paper explicitly points to financial engineering, quantitative trading, and insurance mathematics as application areas, and it mentions extreme market events such as flash crashes and discontinuous price movements. It also says ruin theory is central to insurance mathematics and market microstructure.
business_stakes_quotes:
Furthermore, the storage of the entire path is
absent, leading to crucial practical problems for financial engineering, quantitative trading,
and many other path-dependent scenarios.

The last term on the right hand side represents the discontinuous price movements caused
by such as acquisitions, mergers, corporate scandals, and fat-finger errors.
The ruin theory plays a central role in insurance mathematics, high-frequency trading’s market micro-structure theory, and option pricing [43–46].
extraction_notes: Motivation is explicit in abstract, introduction, and application sections; finance framing is clear and includes both derivative pricing and Monte Carlo/path-dependent analysis.
